var1.description: Index of the location used as the depot.

var2.name: tour_A
var2.description: The sequence of location indices for truck A, starting at warehouse A.
var2.example: For example, `tour_A=[0, 1, ...]` means truck A visits locations in the order of 0,1 and so on.

var3.name: tour_B
var3.description: The sequence of location indices for truck B, starting at warehouse B.
var3.example: For example, `tour_B=[6, 7, ...]` means truck B visits locations in the order of 6,7 and so on.

var4.name: distance
var4.description: Total distance travlelled by the truck with the longest route.

59.name: FreePizza
59.content: The problem arises in the University College Cork student dorms. There is a large order of pizzas for a party, and many of the students have vouchers for acquiring discounts in purchasing pizzas. A voucher is a pair of numbers e.g. (2, 4), which means if you pay for 2 pizzas then you can obtain for free up to 4 pizzas as long as they each cost no more than the cheapest of the 2 pizzas you paid for. Similarly, a voucher (3, 2) means that if you pay for 3 pizzas you can get up to 2 pizzas for free as long as they each cost no more than the cheapest of the 3 pizzas you paid for. The aim is to obtain all the ordered pizzas for the least possible cost. Note that not all vouchers need to be used.

n.description: The number of pizzas to order, given as an integer.

prices.description: List of integers representing prices for each pizza.

buy.description: List of integers where `buy[i]` is the number of pizzas that must be paid for to use the i-th voucher.

free.description: List of integers where `free[i]` is the number of free pizzas asllowed for the i-th voucher.

var1.name: voucher_usage
var1.description: A list representing voucher usage for all pizzas, where entry j indicates how pizza j is paid for: -i-1 if pizza j is a paid pizza for voucher i (0-based), i+1 if pizza j is a free pizza on voucher i, and 0 if pizza j is paid without a voucher.
var1.example: For example, `voucher_usage=[-1, 0, 1, -2]` means pizza 0 is paid with voucher 0, pizza 1 is paid without a voucher, pizza 2 is a free pizza on voucher 1, and pizza 3 is paid with voucher 2.

var2.name: cost
var2.description: The total price paid for the pizzas.

60.name: KidneyExchange
60.content:
In a kidney exchange program, there are `n` patient-donor pairs. Each pair consists of a patient who needs a kidney and a willing donor who is not compatible with their own patient but may be compatible with another patient in the pool. A directed compatibility graph is given, where an arc from node `i` to node `j` indicates that the donor in pair `i` can donate a kidney to the patient in pair `j`. Each arc has a weight, representing the quality or priority of that donation.
The objective is to find a set of node-disjoint cycles (each cycle representing a sequence of patient-donor pairs exchanging kidneys), such that:
(1) Each cycle involves at most `k` pairs 
(2) Each pair participates in at most one cycle (no donor gives a kidney unless their patient receives one). 
(3) No incompatible matches are used. 
(4) The sum of the weights of the selected transplants is maximized.

n.description: Number of patient-donor pairs (size of the weights matrix), given as an integer.

weights.description: A 2D array of integers representing the weights, where `weights[i][j]` is the benefit if donor `i` donates to patient `j`. Negative if incompatible.

k.description: Maximum allowed cycle length, given as an integer.

var1.name: successors
var1.description: A list of integers where `successors[i]=j` means the donor in pair `i` donates to the patient in pair `j`.
var1.example: For example, `successors=[1, 0, ...]` means donor 0 donates to patient 1 and so on.

var2.name: benefit
var2.description: The total sum of weights of the selected transplants.

61.name: TSP_TW
61.content:
Given a set of `n` locations and their pairwise distances, a salesman must visit each customer exactly once, starting and ending at a depot (node 0). Each customer `i` has a time window `[e_i, l_i]`: the salesman must start service at `i` no earlier than `e_i` and no later than `l_i`. The travel time from customer `i` to customer `j` is equal to the distance between `i` and `j`, and the salesman must leave enough time for travel between visits. The objective is to find a tour of minimum total travel distance that: 
(1) Starts and ends at the depot (node 0), 
(2) Visits every customer exactly once, 
(3) Service each customer within their allowed time window, 
(4) The salesman is allowed to arrive at a customer before the window opens, but must wait until the window opens to start service.

n.description: The total number of nodes (including depot), given as an integer.

distances.description: A 2D (n by n) array of integers where `distances[i][j]` gives travel distance from node `i` to node `j`. Node 0 is the depot.

windows.description: A 2D (n by 2) array of time windows, where windows[i] = [earliest, latest] allowed time to visit node i. Node 0 is the depot.

var1.name: tour
var1.description: List of node indices representing the order of visits.
var1.example: For example, `tour=[0,2,1,...,0]` means the salesman starts at node 0, then visits node 2, and so on, and finally returns to node 0.

var2.name: service_times
var2.description: List of integers representing service start time at each node (excluding the return to depot), where `service_times[i]` is the service start time at node `i`.
var2.example: For example, `service_times=[0, 5, 3, ...]` means the salesman is at depot at time 0, starts service at node 1 at time 5, node 2 at time 3, and so on.

var3.name: distance
var3.description: The total distance traveled in the tour.

62.name: OpenShop
62.content:
You are tasked with scheduling a set of jobs on a set of machines. Each job consists of a collection of tasks, where each task is assigned to a specific machine and must be processed for a given duration. For each job, the tasks within it can be processed in any order. Your objective is to determine the start time for each task to minimize the makespan which is defined as the total time elapsed from the start of the first task to the completion of the last task. The following rules must be followed: 
(1) Each job is made up of a series of tasks; each task is assigned to a specific machine and requires exclusive use that machine for its entire duration.  
(2) Once a task starts, it must run to completion without interruption. 
(3) For each job, only one of its tasks can be in progress at any time. 
(4) Each machine can process only one task at a time.

m.description: Number of machines available, given as an integer.

n.description: Number of jobs, given as an integer.

durations.description: A 2D (n by m) array of integers where durations[i][j] is the duration of the j-th task of job i, to be run on machine j.

var1.name: start_times
var1.description: A 2D array representing the assigned start times, where start_times[i][j] is the start time of the j-th task of job i.
var1.example: For example, `start_times=[[0,5,...],...]` means the first task of job 0 starts at time 0, the second task of job 0 starts at time 5, and so on.

var2.name: makespan
var2.description: Total time elapsed from the start of the first task to the completion of the last task.

63.name: TPP
63.content: A grid-based travelling purchaser problem. The goal is to decide where to buy each of a set of products, and in which order to visit the purchase locations, so as to minimize the total travel and purchase costs (products are available at every city for different prices). Travel costs are  asymmetric, and cities are laid out on a grid with travel only allowed between horizontally and vertically adjacent cities.

n.description: Number of products to purchase, given as an integer.

c.description: Number of cities, given as an integer. (depot included)

distances.description: A 2D (c by c) array where `distances[i][j]` is the travel cost from city i to city j. -1 means not allowed.

prices.description: A 2D (c-1 by n) array where `prices[i][j]` is the price of product i in city j.

maxDistance.description: Maximum travel distance allowed for the purchaser, given as an integer.

maxPrice.description: Maximum allowed price for any product, given as an integer.

var1.name: tour
var1.description: Ordered list of city indices representing the order of visits, starting and ending at the depot (city 0). If the actual tour uses fewer than c+1 entries, the remaining entries must be padded with 0.
var1.example: For example, `tour=[0,2,1,...,0]` means the purchaser starts at city 0, then visits city 2, and so on.

var2.name: p_locs
var2.description: List of product purchase locations, where `p_locs[i]` is the city index where product i is purchased.
var2.example: For example, `p_locs=[3, 1, 2,...]` means product 3 is purchased in city 0, product 1 in city 1, and so on.

64.name: RectPacking
64.content: The rectangle (square) packing problem consists of squares (bowes) to be put in an enclosing rectangle (container) without overlapping of the squares.

container.description: List of two integers: [width, height] of the container.

n.description: Number of boxes to be packed, given as an integer.

widths.description: List of integers representing widths for each box; widths[i] is the width of box i.

heights.description: List of integers representing heights for each box; heights[i] is the height of box i.

var1.name: locs
var1.description: A 2D list representing the locations of the boxes, where locs[i] = [x, y] is the bottom-left coordinate of box i in the container.
var1.example: For example, `locs=[[3,5], ...]` means box 0 is placed with its bottom-left corner at (3,5) in the container, etc.

65.name: CyclicBandwidth
65.content: Given a graph G with a set of n vertices and a set of edges, the task is to assign a unique integer from the set {0, 1, ..., n-1} to each vertex. This labeling corresponds to placing the graph's vertices onto the nodes of an n-vertex cycle. The goal is to minimize the cyclic bandwidth, which is defined as the maximum cyclic distance between the labels of any two vertices connected by an edge. For a graph with n vertices, the cyclic distance between two labels, label1 and label2, is calculated as: cyclic_distance=min(|label1-label2|,n-|label1-label2|)

n.description: The number of vertices in the graph, given as an integer.

nEdges.description: The number of edges in the graph, given as an integer.

edges.description: A 2D (nEdges, 2) array of integers representing the edges of the graph, where each each inner list [u, v] indicating an edge between vertices u and v.

var1.name: labels
var1.description: `labels[i]` is the label assigned to vertex i.
var1.example: For example, `labels=[0, 1, 2,...]` means vertex 0 is labeled 0, vertex 1 is labeled 1, and so on.

var2.name: cyclic_bandwidth
var2.description: Maximum cyclic distance between the labels of any two connected vertices.

66.name: Problem Amaze
66.content: Given a grid containing some pairs of identical numbers, connect each pair of similar numbers by drawing a line with horizontal or vertical segments, while paying attention to not having crossed lines. Note: Each line is formed by cells labeled with the same unique integer (corresponding to that pair).

n.description: The number of rows in the grid, given as an integer.

m.description: The number of columns in the grid, given as an integer.

points.description: A list of pairs of 1-based indexing coordinates, each representing the two endpoints of a value to be connected. Each pair is a list of two coordinate pairs, where each coordinate pair is of the form [row, col] in 1-based indexing.
points.example: For example, `points = [[[1,2],[3,4]], [[5,6],[7,8]]]` shows two endpoint paris: the first has endpoints at (1,2) and (3,4), the second at (5,6) and (7,8), and so on.

var1.name: grid
var1.description: An n by m 2D array where each entry is either 0 (unused cell) or an integer representing the value of a path. Each value occurs on a continuous path connecting its two endpoints.
var1.example: For instance, `grid=[[1, 1, 0, ...], [0, 1, 0, ...], ...]` shows value 1 forming a valid path connecting a pair of poins (1,1) and (2,1) on the grid.

67.name: Problem AnotherMagicSquare
67.content: On a square grid of size (n, n), all numbers ranging from 1 to n*n must be put so that the numbers surrounding each number add to a multiple of that number.

n.description: The size of the square grid, given as an integer.

var1.name: grid
var1.description: An n by n 2D array representing the placement of the integers.

68.name: Problem AntimagicSquare
68.content: An anti-magic square of order n is an arrangement of the numbers 1 to n*n in a square, such that the sums of the n rows, the n columns and the two main diagonals form a sequence of 2n + 2 consecutive integers.

n.description: The order of the square, given as an integer.

var1.name: grid
var1.description: An n by n 2D array representing the placement of the integers 1 to n*n in the square.

69.name: Problem Audrey
69.content:
Draw a n cells by n cells board. The purpose is to fill in all cells with numbers from 0 to n^2-1. You start by writing 0 in whatever cell. From there on, you need to write the 1 by moving around in one of the following ways:
- Move by 3 cells horizontally or vertically 
- Or move by 2 cells diagonally 
Then, starting from the 1, you need to write the 2 using the same permitted moves, and so on. The sequence must form a closed circuit, meaning that after writing n^2-1, the cell containing n^2-1 must also be able to move back to the cell containing 0 using one of the same permitted moves.

n.description: The size of the board, given as an integer.

var1.name: grid
var1.description: An n by n 2D array where each cell stores the step number indicating when the circuit visits that cell.
var1.example: For instance, `grid=[[0,1,2,...],...]` represents circut vists (0,0) first, then (0,1), and so on.

70.name: Problem BinPacking
70.content: The bin packing problem (BPP) can be informally defined in a very simple way. We are given n items, each having an integer weight wj (j = 1, ..., n), and an unlimited number of identical bins of integer capacity c. The objective is to pack all the items into the minimum number of bins so that the total weight packed in any bin does not exceed the capacity.

binCapacity.description: The maximum capacity of each bin, given as an integer.

nItems.description: The total number of items to be packed, given as an integer.

itemWeights.description: A list of integers representing the weights of each item.

var1.name: bins
var1.description: List of bin assignments for each item, where `bins[j]` is the index of the bin to which item j is assigned. The bins are 0 indexed.
var1.example: For example, `bins=[0, 1, 0, ...]` means item 0 is assigned to bin 0, item 1 is assigned to bin 1, and so on.

var2.name: num_bins
var2.description: Total number of bins used.

71.name: Problem BinaryPuzzle
71.content:
A binary puzzle (also known as a binary Sudoku) is a puzzle played on an n by n grid.
One has to fill the remaining empty cells with either 0 or 1 according to the following rules:
  -  no more than two similar numbers next to or below each other are allowed,
  -  each row and each column should contain an equal number of zeros and ones,
  - each row is unique and each column is unique.

n.description: The size of the grid, given as an even integer.

var1.name: grid
var1.description: An n by n 2D array representing the filled puzzle grid, where each entry is 0 or 1.

72.name: Problem CalvinPuzzle
72.content:
The purpose of the game is to fill a grid of size n by n with all values ranging from 1 to n*n such that:
  - if the next number in the sequence is going to be placed vertically or horizontally, then it must be placed exactly three squares away
  from the previous number (there must be a two square gap between the numbers);
  - if the next number in the sequence is going to be placed diagonally, then it must be placed exactly two squares away
  from the previous number (there must be a one square gap between the numbers).

n.description: The size of the square grid, given as an integer.

var1.name: grid
var1.description: An n by n 2D array representing the step number placed in each cell.
var1.example: For instance, `grid=[[1,2,...],...]` means (0,0) is visited first, then (0,1), and so on.

73.name: Problem Cutstock
73.content: We are given N items with associated lengths and demands. We are further given stock pieces with length L and an upper bound K on the number of required stock pieces for satisfying the demand (a trivial upper bound is the sum over all the demands). The objective is to minimize the number of stock pieces used.

N.description: The maximum number of stock pieces available, given as an integer.

L.description: The length of each stock piece, given as an integer.

nItems.description: The number of different item types, given as an integer.

i_length.description: A list of integers representing the lengths of each item type.
i_length.example: For example, `i_length=[1,2,...]` means item type 0 has length 1, item type 2 has length 2, and so on.

i_demand.description: A list of integers representing the demand for each item type.
i_demand.example: For example, `i_demand=[3,0,...]` means 3 items of type 0 are needed, no items of type 1 are needed, and so on.

var1.name: assignments
var1.description: An 2D array where `assignments[i][j]` is the number of items of type j cut from stock piece i.
var1.example: For example, `assignments=[[2,0,0],[0,1,0],...]` means from stock piece 0 we cut 2 items of type 0, from stock piece 1 we cut 1 item of type 1, and so on.

var2.name: num_pieces
var2.description: The total number of stock pieces used.

74.name: Problem Dominoes
74.content:
1. You are given a board consisting of 7 rows and 8 columns. Each cell contains a number from 0 to 6.
2. The board is made up from using all dominoes starting from 0-0 to 6-6 exactly once.
3. The dominoes cover the board completely, but they don’t overlap.
4. The dominoes may be rotated in any direction, the orientation of the numbers is not significant.

grid.description: A 7 by 8 2D array of integers between 0 and 6 representing the board.

var1.name: placements
var1.description: A list of 28 elements, one for each domino from 0-0, 0-1, up to 6-6. Each element is a list of two coordinates [row, col] giving the positions of the two cells covered by that domino.
var1.example: For example, `placements=[[[0,1],[0,2]], [[1,0],[2,0]], ... ]` means the domino 0-0 covers cells (0,1) and (0,2), the domino 0-1 covers cells (1,0) and (2,0), and so on.

75.name: Problem GraphMaxAcyclic
75.content: Given an edge-weighted directed graph with possibly many cycles, the task is to find an acyclic sub-graph of maximal weight.

nNodes.description: The number of nodes in the directed graph, given as an integer.

arcs.description: A 2D array representing arc weights. arcs[i][j] is the weight of the directed edge from node i to node j, or 0 if no edge exists.
arcs.example: For example, `arcs = [[0,5,0],[0,0,2],...]` means there is an edge from node 0 to node 1 with weight 5, an edge from node 1 to node 2 with weight 2, and so on.

var1.name: selected_arcs
var1.description: An 2D array where `selected_arcs[i][j] = 1` if the arc from node i to node j is part of the solution, and 0 otherwise.
var1.example: For example, `selected_arcs=[[0,1,0],[0,0,1],[0,0,0]]` means arcs (0 -> 1) and (1 -> 2) are selected.

var2.name: total_weight
var2.description: The total weight of the selected acyclic subgraph.

76.name: Problem HCPizza
76.content: The pizza corresponds to a 2-dimensional grid of n rows and m columns. Each cell of the pizza contains either mushroom or tomato. A slice of pizza is a rectangular section of the pizza delimited by two rows and two columns, without holes. The slices we want to cut out must contain at least L cells of each ingredient and at most H cells of any kind in total. The slices being cut out cannot overlap, and do not need to cover the entire pizza. The goal is to cut correct slices out of the pizza maximizing the total number of cells in all slices.

minIngredients.description: The minimum number of each ingredient (mushroom and tomato) required in every slice, given as an integer.

maxSize.description: The maximum number of cells allowed in a slice, given as an integer.

pizza.description: A 2D array representing the pizza grid, where 0 indicates a mushroom and 1 indicates a tomato.
pizza.example: For example, pizza=[[1,0,1],[0,1,0]] represents a 2 by 3 pizza where row 0 is [tomato, mushroom, tomato] and row 1 is [mushroom, tomato, mushroom].

var1.name: slices
var1.description: A list of slices, where each slice is represented as [r1, c1, r2, c2] with (r1,c1) as the top-left cell and (r2,c2) as the bottom-right cell of the slice (inclusive). Coordinates are 0-indexed.
var1.example: For example, slices=[[0,0,1,1],[0,2,2,2]] means the first slice covers rows 0-1 and cols 0-1, the second slice covers rows 0-2 and col 2 only.

var2.name: total_cells
var2.description: The total number of pizza cells included in the selected slices.

77.name: Problem Kakuro
77.content:
The puzzle uses the following rules:
 1. The puzzle uses a rectilinear grid of back and white cells. Black cells may contain hints (integer numbers). The number below the diagonal divider is the hint for cells below, the number above the diagonal divider is the hint for cells to the right.
 2. The task is to enter numbers from 1 to 9 into the white cells satisfying the constraints.
 3. The sum of a continuous block of white cell in horizontal (or vertical) direction must be equal to the hint given in the black cell to the left (above).
 4. All numbers in a continuous block of white cells must be pairwise different.

nRows.description: The number of rows in the grid, given as an integer.

nCols.description: The number of columns in the grid, given as an integer.

row_clues.description: A 2D array of integers, where row_clues[i][j] is the horizontal clue of the black cell at (i,j). Value 0 indicates the cell is white, -1 indicates no horizontal clue.
row_clues.example: For example, `row_clues=[[ -1, 14, -0, ..],[ 27, 0, ..]]` means (0,0) is a black cell with no horizontal clue; (0,1) is a black cell with horizontal clue 14; (0,2) is white, and so on.

col_clues.description: A 2D array of integers, where col_clues[i][j] is the vertical clue of the black cell at (i,j). Value 0 indicates the cell is white, -1 indicates no vertical clue.
col_clues.example: For example, `col_clues=[[ -1, 17, 0, ...],...]` means (0,0) is a black cell with no vertical clue; (0,1) is a black cell with vertical clue 17, and so on .

var1.name: grid
var1.description: A 2D array where each entry is either 0 for black cells or an integer 1-9 for white cells.

78.name: Knapsack Problem
78.content: Given a set of items, each with a mass and a value, determine the number of each item to include in a collection so that the total weight is less than or equal to a given limit and the total value is as large as possible.

capacity.description: The maximum total weight that can be carried, given as an integer.

nItems.description: The total number of items available, given as an integer.

item_weights.description: A list of integers representing the weight of each item.
item_weights.example: For example, `item_weights=[1,5,2]` means there are three items with weights 1, 5, and 2.

item_values.description: A list of integers representing the value of each item.
item_values.example: For example, item_values=[44, 89, 25] means the three items have values 44, 89, and 25 respectively.

var1.name: selected
var1.description: A list of binary values, where `selected[i] = 1` if item i is chosen and 0 otherwise.
var1.example: For example, selected=[1,0,1] means items 0 and 2 are chosen, and item 1 is not.

var2.name: total_value
var2.description: The total value of the selected items.

79.name: Problem Mario
79.content:
Mario is an Italian Plumber and his work is mainly to find gold in the plumbing of all the houses of the neighborhood.
Mario is moving in the city using his kart that has a specified amount of fuel.
Mario starts his day of work from his house and always ends to his friend Luigi's house to have the supper.
The problem here is to plan the best path for Mario in order to earn the more money with the amount of fuel of his kart.

From a more general point of view, the problem is to find a path in a graph:
 - Path endpoints are given (from Mario's to Luigi's)
 - The sum of weights associated to arcs in the path is restricted (fuel consumption)
 - The sum of weights associated to nodes in the path has to be maximized (gold coins)

marioHouse.description: The index of the node corresponding to Mario's house (start of the path).

luigiHouse.description: The index of the node corresponding to Luigi's house (end of the path).

nHouses.description: The total number of houses (nodes) in the neighborhood, given as an integer.

fuelLimit.description: The maximum fuel available for Mario's kart, given as an integer.

fuels.description: A 2D array where fuels[i][j] is the fuel consumption required to travel from house i to house j. A value of 0 means no arc exists.
fuels.example: For example, `fuels=[[0,5,0],[0,0,2],...]` represents a graph with 2 nodes and edges 0->1 (5 fuel), 1->2 (2 fuel), and so on.

golds.description: A list of integers where golds[i] is the gold coins available at house i.
golds.example: For example, `golds=[0,3,0]` means only node 1 contains 3 gold coins.

var1.name: path
var1.description: A list of node indices representing the path from Mario's house to Luigi's house, in visiting order.
var1.example: For example, path=[0,3,2,1] means Mario starts at node 0, visits nodes 3 and 2, and ends at node 1 (Luigi's house).

var2.name: total_gold
var2.description: The total amount of gold collected along the path.

80.name: Problem MineSweeper
80.content: Given a grid with some cells containing numerical clues and others left blank. Each clue indicates the exact number of mines present in the eight surrounding cells. The task is to decide which of the blank cells contain mines so that all the numerical clues are satisfied.

nRows.description: The number of rows in the puzzle grid, given as an integer.

nCols.description: The number of columns in the puzzle grid, given as an integer.

puzzle.description: A 2D array of integers representing the grid. Each entry is either -1 (unknown cell) or a nonnegative integer giving the number of mines in the surrounding cells.
puzzle.example: For example, `puzzle=[[1,-1,2,...],...]` means cell (0,0) has clue 1, cell (0,1) is unknown, and cell (0,2) has clue 2.

var1.name: grid
var1.description: An 2d array where `grid[i][j] = 1` if cell (i,j) contains a mine, and 0 otherwise.
var1.example: For example, `grid=[[0, 1, 0, ...], ...]` means cell (0,1) contains a mine, and so on.

81.name: Problem PerfectSquare
81.content: Pack a set of squares with given integer sizes into a bigger square in such a way that no squares overlap each other and all square borders are parallel to the border of the big square.

size.description: The side length of the large square, given as an integer.

nSquares.description: The total number of smaller squares to be packed, given as an integer.

squares.description: A list of integers representing the side lengths of the smaller squares to be packed.
squares.example: For example, `squares=[1,2,3, ...]` means there are squares with side lengths 1, 2, 3, and so on.

var1.name: placements
var1.description: A list of coordinates giving the bottom-left corner of each placed square. `placements[i] = [x, y]` corresponds to the position of squares[i]. Note: The origin (0,0) is at the bottom-left corner of the large enclosing square
var1.example: For example, placements=[[0,0],[50,0],...] means the first square is placed at (0,0), the second at (50,0), and so on.

82.name: Problem RoomMate
82.content: Given an even number of agents to be matched together as couples, where each agent strictly ranks all other agents. The problem is then to match pairs of agents together such that the matching is stable, i.e. there doesn't exist a pair of agents in the matching such that agent_i prefers agent_j to his matched partner and agent_j prefers agent_i to his matched partner.

n.description: The total number of agents to be matched.

preferences.description: A 2D array of shape `n` by `(n-1)` where `preferences[i]` is the ordered list of all other agents ranked by agent i, from most preferred to least preferred. Agents are 1-based indexed.
preferences.example: For example, `preferences=[[2,3,5,...],[1,3,6,...],...]` means agent 1 prefers 2 > 3 > 5, agent 2 prefers 1 > 3 > 6, and so on.

var1.name: matching
var1.description: A list of integers where `match[i]` is the partner of agent i. Agents are 1-based indexed.
var1.example: For example, `match=[2,1,4,3,...]` means agent 1 is matched with agent 2, agent 2 is matched with agent 1, and so on.

83.name: Problem StableMarriage
83.content:
Consider two groups of men and women who must marry.
Consider that each person has indicated a ranking for her/his possible spouses.
The problem is to find a matching between the two groups such that the marriages are stable.
A marriage between a man m and a woman w is stable iff:
 - whenever m prefers another woman o to w, o prefers her husband to m
 - whenever w prefers another man o to m, o prefers his wife to w

n.description: The number of men (and women) to match.

women_rankings.description: A 2D array of integers where `women_rankings[w][m]` is the rank woman w gives to man m (1 = most preferred, n = least).
women_rankings.example: For example, `women_rankings=[[1,2,3,...],...]` means woman 0 prefers man 0 over man 1 over man 2, and so on.

men_rankings.description: A 2D array of integers where `men_rankings[m][w]` is the rank man m gives to woman w (1 = most preferred, n = least).
men_rankings.example: For example, `men_rankings=[[1,2,3,...],...]` means man 0 prefers woman 0 over woman 1 over woman 2, and so on.

var1.name: women_matching
var1.description: A list of integers where `women_matching[w]` is the 0-based index of the man matched to woman w. Women and men are 0-based indexed.
var1.example: For example, `women_matching=[0,2,1]` means woman 0 is matched with man 0, woman 1 is matched with man 2, and woman 2 is matched with man 1.

84.name: Problem Sudoku
84.content: Sudoku is a puzzle played on a partially filled 9 by 9 grid. The task is to complete the assignment using numbers from 1 to 9 such that the entries in each row, each column and each major 3 by 3 block are pairwise different.

n.description: The order of the grid, given as an integer.

clues.description: A 2d array of shape (n,n) where `clues[i][j]` is the prefilled value at row i, column j. A value of 0 indicates the cell is empty.
clues.example: For example, `clues=[[7,0,3,...],...]` means (0,0) is filled with 7, (0,1) is empty, and so on.

var1.name: grid
var1.description: A 2d array representing the completed assignment. Each entry is in {1..n}.
var1.example: For example, `grid=[[7,8,3,...],...]` means (0,0) is filled with 7, (0,1) is filled with 8, and so on.

85.name: Problem Survo
85.content: The task is to fill an m by n table with integers 1, 2, ..., m*n so that each of these numbers appears only once and their row and column sums are equal to given integers.

m.description: The number of rows in the table.

n.description: The number of columns in the table.

rowSums.description: A list of integers where `rowSums[i]` is the required sum of row i.
rowSums.example: For example, `rowSums=[15, 40, ...]` means row 0 must sum to 15, row 1 must sum to 40, and so on.

colSums.description: A list of integers where `colSums[j]` is the required sum of column j.
colSums.example: For example, `colSums=[12, 30, ...]` means column 0 must sum to 12 and so on.

matrix.description: A 2D array representing the initial state of the table. Empty cells are represented by 0.
matrix.example: For example, `matrix=[[0,6,0...],...]` means (0,0) is empty, (0,1) has a fixed number of 6, and so on.

var1.name: grid
var1.description: A 2D array representing the completed assignment of integers in the table.
var1.example: For example, `grid=[[5,6,7...],...]` means (0,0) is filled with 5, (0,1) is filled with 6, and so on.

86.name: Problem TrainSchedule
86.content:
The SNCB finally decided to rely on optimization technologies to schedule the departure of its fleet at Brussels central. The problem to be solved is the following:
- Each train has a scheduled departure time.
- If a train departs earlier or later than expected, a penalty cost is incurred per time unit.
- After a train has left the station, no other train can depart for a given period (number of time units, or 'gap', which depends upon the train that has left).
- The goal is to minimize the cost incurred by early and late departs.

n.description: The total number of trains to be scheduled, given as an integer.

trains.description: A list of triples [scheduled_time, gap, cost_per_time_unit], one for each train.
trains.example: For example, `trains=[[890, 5, 2], [683, 3, 1], ...]` means train 0 has scheduled time 890, requires an 5-unit gap, and costs 2 per deviation, and so on.

var1.name: schedule
var1.description: A list of integers where `departures[i]` is the actual departure time assigned to train i.
var1.example: For example, `schedule=[395,687,899, ...]` means train 0 leaves at time 395, train 1 at 687, and so on.

var2.name: total_cost
var2.description: The total penalty cost incurred by deviations from scheduled departure times.

87.name: Problem TravelingSalesman
87.content: Given a list of cities and the distances between each pair of cities, what is the shortest possible route that visits each city exactly once and returns to the origin city?

n.description: The total number of cities, given as an integer.

distances.description: A square 2D array where `distances[i][j]` is the distance from city i to city j (0 on the diagonal).
distances.example: For example, `distances=[[0,3,15,...],...]` means the distance from city 0 to city 1 is 3, from city 0 to city 2 is 15, and so on.

var1.name: tour
var1.description: A list of city indices in visit order. The tour goes through tour[0], tour[1], ..., tour[n-1] and then returns to tour[0].
var1.example: For instance, `tour=[0,2,1,3]` means the sequence of visited cities is 0 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 -> 0.

var2.name: z
var2.description: The total length of tour.

88.name: Problem Abbots
88.content: We know that 100 bushels of corn were distributed among 100 people. Each man received three bushels, each woman two, and each child half a bushel. There are five times as many women as men. How many men, women, and children were there?

var1.name: m
var1.description: An integer giving the number of men.

var2.name: w
var2.description: An integer giving the number of women.

var3.name: c
var3.description: An integer giving the number of children.

89.name: Problem Agatha
89.content:
Someone who lives in Dreadsbury Mansion killed Aunt Agatha.
Agatha, the butler, and Charles live in Dreadsbury Mansion, and are the only people who live therein.
We know that:
 - A killer always hates his victim, and is never richer than his victim.
 - Charles hates no one that Aunt Agatha hates.
 - Agatha hates everyone except the butler.
 - The butler hates everyone not richer than Aunt Agatha.
 - The butler hates everyone Agatha hates.
 - No one hates everyone.

var1.name: killer
var1.description: An integer index of the person who killed Agatha (0 = Agatha, 1 = Butler, 2 = Charles).

var2.name: hating
var2.description: A 3 by 3 array where hating[i][j] is 1 if person i hates person j, else 0.

var3.name: richer
var3.description: A 3 by 3 array where richer[i][j] is 1 if person i is richer than person j, else 0.

90.name: Problem Allergy
90.content:
Four friends are two women named Debra and Janet, and two men named Hugh and Rick.
They found that each of them is allergic to something different: eggs, mold, nuts and ragweed.
We would like to match each one's surname (Baxter, Lemon, Malone and Fleet) with his or her allergy.
We know that:
 - Rick is not allergic to mold
 - Baxter is allergic to eggs
 - Hugh is neither surnamed Lemon nor Fleet
 - Debra is allergic to ragweed
 - Janet (who isn't Lemon) is neither allergic to eggs nor to mold

var1.name: allergic
var1.description: A list of length 4 where allergic[a] is the index of the friend who has allergy a. Use friend indices [0: Debra, 1: Janet, 2: Hugh, 3: Rick] and allergy indices [0: eggs, 1: mold, 2: nuts, 3: ragweed].
var1.example: For instance, `allergic=[0, 3, 1, 2]` means Debra is allergic to eggs, Rick is allergic to mold, Hugh is allergic to nuts, and Janet is allergic to ragweed.

var2.name: surnames
var2.description: A list where `surnames[i]` is the index of the friend who has surname s. Use friend indices [0: Debra, 1: Janet, 2: Hugh, 3: Rick] and surname indices [0: Baxter, 1: Lemon, 2: Malone, 3: Fleet].
var2.example: For instance, `surnames=[0, 1, 2, 3]` means Debra's surname is Baxter, Janet's surname is Lemon, Hugh's surname is Malone, and so on .

91.name: Problem Photo
91.content:
Betty, Chris, Donald, Fred, Gary, Mary, and Paul want to align in one row for taking a photo.
Some of them have preferences next to whom they want to stand:
 - Betty wants to stand next to Gary and Mary.
 - Chris wants to stand next to Betty and Gary.
 - Fred wants to stand next to Mary and Donald.
 - Paul wants to stand next to Fred and Donald.

var1.name: lineup
var1.description: A list of length 7 giving the order of friends from left to right in the photo. The friends are indexed as [0: Betty, 1: Chris, 2: Donald, 3: Fred, 4: Gary, 5: Mary, 6: Paul].
var1.example: For instance, `lineup=[0, 3, 1,...]` means Betty is leftmost, followed by Fred, Chris, and so on.

var2.name: unsatisfied
var2.description: The number of adjacency preferences that are not satisfied in the final arrangement.

92.name: Problem Square
92.content: There is one four-digit whole number x, such that the last four digits of x^2 are in fact the original number x. What is it?

var1.name: x
var1.description: The four-digit integer satisfying the requirement.

93.name: Problem Sandwich
93.content:
Someone in the university ate Alice's sandwich at the cafeteria. We want to find out who the culprit is.
The witnesses are unanimous about the following facts:
 - Three persons were in the cafeteria at the time of the crime: Alice, Bob, and Sascha.
 - The culprit likes Alice.
 - The culprit is taller than Alice.
 - Nobody is taller than himself.
 - If A is taller than B, then B is not taller than A.
 - Bob likes no one that Alice likes.
 - Alice likes everybody except Bob.
 - Sascha likes everyone that Alice likes.
 - Nobody likes everyone.

var1.name: culprit
var1.description: An integer index indicating the culprit. Use 0 for Alice, 1 for Bob, 2 for Sascha.

var2.name: liking
var2.description: A 3 by 3 array where `liking[i][j] = 1` if person i likes person j, and 0 otherwise.  Indices 0,1,2 map to Alice, Bob, Sascha respectively.
var2.example: For example, `liking=[[0,0,1],...]` indicates Alice likes Sascha and so on.

var3.name: taller
var3.description: A 3 by 3 array where `taller[i][j] = 1` if person i is taller than person j, and 0 otherwise. Indices 0,1,2 map to Alice, Bob, Sascha respectively.
var3.example: For example, `taller=[[0,0,1],...]` indicates Alice is taller than Sascha and so on.

94.name: Problem SafeCracking
94.content:
The code of Professor Smart's safe is a sequence of 9 distinct
nonzero digits d1 .. d9 such that the following equations and
inequations are satisfied:
```
  d4 - d6 = d7
  d1 * d2 * d3 = d8 + d9
  d2 + d3 + d6 < d8
  d9 < d8
  d1 <> 1, d2 <> 2, ..., d9 <> 9
```
Can you find the correct combination?

var1.name: digits
var1.description: An array of nine digits representing d1..d9 in order.
var1.example: For example, `digits=[2,3,4,...]` indicates d1=2, d2=3, and so on.

95.name: Problem Purdey
95.content:
One morning, in 1880, four families (the Boyds, Garveys, Logans and Navarros) stopped by Purdey's general store.
Each family bought a different item: 50 pounds of flour, two gallons of kerosene, ten yards of muslin cloth, ten pounds of sugar.
One family paid cash, one took the item on credit and the other two traded other items for it (one a cured ham and the other a bushel of peas).
We know that:
 - the Boyds were new in town, and this was their first visit to the store
 - the family (which wasn't the Logans) that traded the bushel of peas didn't buy the kerosene
 - the Boyds and the Garveys bought the kerosene and the muslin in some order
 - one family traded a cured ham for a large sack of flour
 - Purdey only extended credit to regular customers, such as the family that bought the muslin on credit

var1.name: payment_family
var1.description: A list of length 4 where `payment_family[p]` is the index of the family who used payment method p. Use payment indices [0: cash, 1: credit, 2: ham, 3: peas] and family indices [0: Boyds, 1: Garveys, 2: Logans, 3: Navarros].
var1.example: For instance, `payment_family=[0, 1, 2, 3]` means the Boyds paid cash, the Garveys paid on credit, the Logans traded a ham, and the Navarros traded peas.

var2.name: item_buyer
var2.description: A list of length 4 where item_buyer[i] is the index of the family who bought item i. Use item indices [0: flour, 1: kerosene, 2: muslin, 3: sugar] and family indices [0: Boyds, 1: Garveys, 2: Logans, 3: Navarros].
var2.example: For instance, `item_buyer=[0,1,2,3]` means the Boyds got flour, the Garveys got kerosene, the Logans got muslin, and so on.

96.name: Problem OPD
96.content: An OPD problem $\langle v, b, r \rangle$ is to find a matrix of $v$ rows and $b$ columns of $0$-$1$ values such that each row sums to $r$, and the maximum, denoted $\lambda$, of the dot products between all pairs of distinct rows is minimal.

v.description: Number of rows in the matrix.

b.description: Number of columns in the matrix.

var1.name: matrix
var1.description: A 2d binary array representing the solution.

var2.name: lambda_val
var2.description: An integer giving the maximum dot product over all pairs of distinct rows of the matrix.

97.name: Problem Blackhole
97.content: A one-player card game played with a standard set of 52 cards. The goal is to play all the cards into the 'Black Hole' pile. Initially the black hole has one card, the ace of spades, and the remaining 51 cards are arranged in 17 fans of 3 cards.  The fans are face-up, so the value of all cards can be seen at all times. Cards are played one by one from the top of a fan into the black hole. To play a card into the black hole, the card must be adjacent in rank to the card on top of the black hole (i.e., exactly one rank higher or lower than the current top card, suits are ignored; Ace is adjacent to King). Note: This task may not use a 52-card deck; the deck contains 4*nCardsPerSuit cards in total.

nCardsPerSuit.description: The number of ranks per suit. The total number of cards is then 4 * nCardsPerSuit.

piles.description: List of piles (fans), each a list of card IDs from top to bottom. Card 0 (the fixed initial black-hole card) must not appear in any pile.
piles.example: For instance, `piles=[[1, 4, 13], ...]` means the first fan contains cards 1, 4, and 13.

var1.name: stack
var1.description: An array listing card IDs in play order. Index 0 is the fixed initial card (ID 0).
var1.example: For instance, `stack=[0, 9, 3, ...]` means after the initial card 0, card 9 is played, then card 3, and so on.

98.name: Rack Configuration Problem
98.content:
racks with electronic connectors. Each card plugged into a rack uses a connector. In order to plug a card into a rack, the rack must be of a rack model.
Each card is characterised by the power it requires. Each rack model is characterised by the maximal power it can supply, its number of connectors, and its price. The problem is to decide how many of the available racks are actually needed, and which rack is of which rack model such that
- every card is plugged into one rack
- the total power demand and the number of connectors required by the cards does not exceed that available for a rack
- the total price is minimised.

nRacks.description: Maximum number of rack slots available, given as an integer.

nCardTypes.description: Number of available card types, given as an integer.

nModels.description: Number of available rack models, given as an integer.

models.description: List of available rack models; each subarray is [power_capacity, connector_count, cost].
models.example: For example, `models=[[150,8,150],...]` means model 0 supplies 150 power with 8 connectors at a cost of 150.

cardTypes.description: List of card types; each type is [power_required, demand]. Demand is the number of cards of this type that must be placed.
cardTypes.example: For instance, `cardTypes=[[20,10],...]` means 10 cards need 20 power each.

var1.name: model_of_rack
var1.description: A list representing the model assigned to each rack, where `model_of_rack[i]` is the model index (0..nModels-1) assigned to rack i, or -1 if rack i is unused.
var1.example: For instance, `model_of_rack=[1, -1, 0, ...]` leaves racks 1 unused, assigns model 1 to rack 0, model 0 to racks 2, and so on.

var2.name: cards_in_rack
var2.description: A 2d array where `cards_in_rack[i][j]` is the number of cards of type j placed in rack i.
var2.example: For instance, `cards_in_rack=[[5,3],[0,0]]` means rack 0 holds five cards of type 0 and three of type 1, rack 1 is empty.

var3.name: total_cost
var3.description: The sum of costs of models chosen for all used racks

99.name: Sports Tournament Scheduling
99.content: The problem is to schedule a tournament of $n$ teams over $n-1$ weeks, with each week divided into $n/2$ periods, and each period divided into two slots. The first team in each slot plays at home, whilst the second plays the first team away. A tournament must satisfy the following three constraints: every team plays once a week; every team plays at most twice in the same period over the tournament; every team plays every other team.

n.description: The (even) number of teams to schedule.

var1.name: home
var1.description: A 2d array of team indices; `home[w][p]` is the home team scheduled in week w, period p. Team indices start at 0.
var1.example: For instance, `home=[[0,2],[1,3],...]` means week 0 period 0 has team 0 at home, week 0 period 1 has team 2 at home, and so on.

var2.name: away
var2.description: A 2d array of team indices; `away[w][p]` is the away team scheduled in week w, period p. Team indices start at 0.
var2.example: For instance, `away=[[1,3],[0,2],...]` means week 0 and period 0 has team 1 away and so on.

100.name: Problem CVRP
100.content: Given a fixed number of identical vehicles and a set of nodes consisting of a single depot and multiple customers, design a set of vehicle routes to minimize total travel distance. Each route starts and ends at the depot, and each customer is visited exactly once by exactly one vehicle. The demand of the customers served on any single route must not exceed the vehicle capacity.

nNodes.description: Number of nodes including the depot.

demands.description: A list where `demand[0]=0` for the depot, and `demand[i]` is the demand of customer i.

distances.description: An 2d array where `distances[i][j]` is the travel cost from node i to node j (0 on the diagonal).

var1.name: routes
var1.description: A 2D array of node indices, where `routes[v][k]` is the k-th node on vehicle v's route. Use 0 as padding after the last customer for that vehicle.
var1.example: For instance, `routes=[[0,4,2,0,0,0],[0,1,3,5,0,0]]` means vehicle 0 leaves depot, visits customers 4 then 2, returns to depot; vehicle 1 visits customers 1, then 3, then 5.

var2.name: total_distance
var2.description: Total travel distance over all vehicle tours (including depot departures and returns).
